Positive derivatives and canonical representatives

Reconstructed by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Earlier edition by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI). Original exposition: CC0. Linked programme prerequisites retain their stated licences. Self-checked by the writing AI.

A distribution does not choose a value at a single point. Positivity can nevertheless select a particular representative. A positive first derivative produces an increasing function, a positive Hessian produces a finite continuous convex function, and a positive Laplacian produces an upper semicontinuous function recovered by its shrinking sphere averages. In the last case the selected value can be minus infinity.

All positivity statements concern real distributions, meaning real values on real tests. We use the positive-measure proof in Order, positivity and distributional limits, Theorem 4.1; the flux and surface measure in Boundary flux and weak identities, Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 2.2; the all-dimensional harmonic distribution lemma in Cauchy kernels and boundary limits; the Laplacian source in Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, Theorem 1.1; and the compact-factor convolution, parameter and local approximation proofs in Convolution as addition of supports, B0–B3, Theorem 1.1, Proposition 5.1 and Theorem 5.2. Polar integration, sphere scaling and constants are proved in the supplied angular foundations, A4–A5. Precise free human-source comparisons are listed at the end.

Two elementary identification facts will be useful. If on an open interval , every compact smooth test of integral zero has a compact primitive in : integrate from the left of its support; the zero integral makes the primitive vanish on the right as well. Thus . Choose of integral one and apply this to . It gives , so is constant.

Also, a locally integrable function with zero distribution is zero almost everywhere. On a compact , multiply it by a compact cutoff equal to one near , and extend by zero to obtain an function . Its small smooth averages vanish on , since there they pair the original zero distribution with compact tests. The approximation theorem in the integration foundations, §15.4, gives . An exhaustion by compact sets proves the assertion. Consequently two locally integrable representatives of a distribution agree almost everywhere; if they are continuous, they agree everywhere, because a nonzero continuous difference has a nonzero sign on a ball of positive volume.

Positive slopes are cumulative measures

Increasing always means nondecreasing. Jump values are not determined by a distribution; we select the right-continuous convention.

Conversely, average an increasing locally bounded function with a nonnegative compact smooth unit-mass kernel. On every smaller interval the averages are increasing: compare the translated arguments under their integrals. They are smooth by the local convolution theorem, so their first derivatives are nonnegative. Their distributional limit is the original function. Testing the derivative limit on any nonnegative compact test proves positivity.

For complex distributions, a positive first derivative leaves an imaginary constant, and a positive second derivative leaves an imaginary affine function. This follows by applying the zero-derivative fact to the imaginary part once or twice; Solution 2 gives the precise statements.

A positive Laplacian selects one function

A function is upper semicontinuous if is open for every real . It is then Borel measurable and bounded above on compact sets: choose a local finite upper bound at each point and use a finite subcover. On a nonempty compact set its supremum is attained. Unless all values are , choose a sequence approaching the finite supremum, take a convergent subsequence, and apply upper semicontinuity.

We call subharmonic when it is upper semicontinuous, is not identically on any connected component, and satisfies

The sphere integral initially has an extended value: its positive part is bounded on that compact sphere, and its negative part may have infinite integral.

Proof. A nonempty compact subset of , , has nonempty boundary: a ray from a point eventually leaves the bounded set and has a last initial point in it. If is throughout , the equality follows. Otherwise its finite maximum is attained. If a maximum point is interior to , let . Compactness of the boundary attains this distance; the closed ball lies in , and its sphere meets .

Positive Hessians force convexity

On an arbitrary open set, convexity here means the chord inequality on every segment contained in that set; the domain itself need not be convex.

Theorem 4.1 (the distributional Hessian criterion). For a real distribution on open , the following are equivalent: every directional second derivative , , is positive; and has a finite continuous representative satisfying

whenever . The representative is unique and locally Lipschitz.

Proof. The directional condition in the coordinate directions implies . Let be the canonical representative and smooth with a nonnegative radial kernel. Each directional second derivative of is a positive distribution paired with a nonnegative translated kernel, hence is a nonnegative smooth function. Restricting to a segment, the fundamental theorem makes the first derivative increasing; its ordered secant slopes prove the chord inequality.

Any compact segment in has positive distance from . For small the preceding argument applies to it. Corollary 3.3 lets in the chord inequality, initially with possible endpoint values. If either endpoint tends to , its positive coefficient forces the right side to , since the other endpoint has a finite upper bound. Thus the extended inequality also holds.

There are in fact no points. If , choose a ball about in . Almost every in it has finite, by local integrability. The midpoint inequality forces . Affine change of variables shows that these midpoints fill almost all of a smaller ball of positive volume, contradicting integrability.

Choose and a finite upper bound for on it. For , apply the midpoint inequality to :

For distinct with , put . Ordered secant slopes on the line through bound the slope from to between and . If , use that endpoint slope directly. Therefore

For , the oscillation bound proves the same inequality; for it is immediate. This proves local Lipschitz continuity.

Conversely, on a compactly contained ball, smooth the continuous chord-convex with a nonnegative kernel. Every sufficiently small translate of a segment in a smaller ball stays inside ; integrating its chord inequality proves convexity of the smoothing there. Symmetric second differences give each smooth directional second derivative nonnegative. Distributional convergence yields positivity on every nonnegative test supported in that ball. A finite nonnegative smooth partition of a general compact test among such balls proves positivity on . The identification fact gives uniqueness of the continuous representative.

Solution 4. Both are zero almost everywhere, hence have zero distributional Laplacian. The upward spike is upper semicontinuous but violates submean at zero, where every circle mean is zero. Programme proof locations and freely accessible sources

  • Order, positivity and distributional limits, Theorem 4.1, and its supplied positive-measure foundation: the full positive Radon representation proof. The zero-derivative and locally integrable identification arguments used here are supplied at the start of this lesson.
  • Boundary flux and weak identities, Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 2.2: graph surface measure, flux and Green identity. Angular foundations, A4–A5: polar integration, sphere scaling and exact constants.
  • Cauchy kernels and boundary limits, “Local smoothing for both constant symbols,” harmonic distribution lemma: smooth harmonic representatives on every open subset of every , including .
  • Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, Theorem 1.1: the exact positive Laplacian sources and their locally integrable first derivatives. Convolution as addition of supports, B0–B3, Theorem 1.1, Proposition 5.1 and Theorem 5.2: compact-factor convolution, parameter tests, derivative transfer and local smoothing.
  • Integration foundations, §§15.0–15.4 and 16.1–16.2: convergence, affine changes, approximation and product-measure Tonelli/Fubini. Scalar foundations, §§12–13, and finite algebra, §§10.1–10.6, supply the compactness, calculus, cutoff and Euclidean norm facts.
  • Dale Winter, notes prepared in collaboration with Tobias Holck Colding, Lecture One: Harmonic Functions and the Harnack Inequality, MIT, 2005, free course notes, §4, pp. 3–4. The smooth sphere-mean derivative and boundary-maximum arguments are compared here.
  • Potential Theory in the Complex Plane, student write-up of Tobias Mai's Saarland University course, summer 2020, free university-hosted notes, Theorem V.4, Corollary V.10 and Theorems VI.2–VI.4. These supply comparison arguments for local integrability, pointwise recovery and positive potentials; the present lesson proves its normalization, smoothing, singular sphere estimates and canonical construction in full.
